title: Equanimity
hook: the tenth perfection: balance in all conditions
tomorrow: how do you talk someone out of a bad idea without a fight?

segments.voice: Yesterday was a day of kindness: every hour, small as a linchpin. Kindness moves toward people. Today's perfection holds still.

The group chat loves your post at noon. By five, someone has screenshotted it with a snarky caption. Same post. Same you. Different weather. So how do you stay level? The Buddha has a list for exactly this, and it's older than any feed: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. The eight worldly conditions, he calls them. They spin after the world, he says, and the world spins after them.
screen: `LOVED AT NOON. MOCKED BY FIVE.` → `SAME YOU, DIFFERENT WEATHER.` → `THE EIGHT WORLDLY CONDITIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the surprise in that sutta: nobody gets out of the weather. The one who has heard the teaching and the one who hasn't both meet praise and blame. The difference is what happens next. When praise comes, the one who has heard reflects: this has come, and it doesn't last; it's subject to change. Blame gets the same reflection. And so neither one takes over the mind. The Pali word is upekkha, equanimity: balance, an even mind. It isn't not caring. It's caring without being thrown. The Dhammapada gives it one picture, in Max Müller's translation: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." The wind still blows. The rock is still a rock. Look at what that does with blame, the hard half. It doesn't wave blame away. A rock still hears the wind. If the blame is true, fix the thing. If it isn't, let it pass. Either way, it doesn't get to tell you who you are. And praise gets the very same treatment. Enjoy it, say thanks, and don't build a house on it.
screen: `NOBODY GETS OUT OF THE WEATHER.` · `IT COMES; IT'S SUBJECT TO CHANGE.` · `A ROCK NOT SHAKEN BY THE WIND.` · `TRUE BLAME: FIX IT. PRAISE: NO HOUSE.` · then, large: `BALANCE.`

segments.voice: Take a pen. On one line, write a recent bit of praise; under it, a recent bit of blame, the same size, in the same calm hand. Read both once, slowly, and let them sit side by side, the way two kinds of weather share one sky.
Upekkha: equanimity, an even mind that stays itself through gain and loss, praise and blame.
Your line: balance. A rock in the wind, the same at noon and at five. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists chant the Mangala Sutta, whose blessings include a mind unshaken when touched by the ways of the world, and equanimity is practiced as one of the four divine abodes, with kindness, compassion and gladness.

fork.setup: your sketch gets a pile of likes, then one stinging comment, and the comment is all you can think about. what does upekkha do?
options: check whether the comment is fair, keep what's true, let the rest pass.
delete the post, so the comment can't sting anymore.
reread the likes until the comment stops mattering.
fork.reveal: upekkha doesn't wave blame away or hide behind praise. it checks what's true and lets the rest blow past, like wind on a rock.

chat.says: yesterday petrov said "best mat cut i've seen." today: "who scratched this glass?" wasn't me. whiplash.
options: Both are weather. Say thanks, check the glass, say plainly it wasn't you.
Hold onto the praise. It proves he's wrong, so just ignore the blame.
Equanimity means not caring. Shrug at both and don't say anything.
chat.meaning: The sutta says praise and blame both come and go. Upekkha meets them evenly: enjoy praise, check blame, and let neither decide who you are.

tie.story: The Buddha said everyone meets praise and blame; whoever sees that they pass isn't taken over by either.
tie.friend: Mai can thank Mr. Petrov for the praise and calmly tell him the scratch wasn't hers.
tie.you: which throws you more lately, praise or blame?
